claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles at high temperature is governed by formation of a stable oxide layer.
The oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier against further oxidation.
The oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier against corrosion.
Annealing at 773–1173 K in inert gas or vacuum will produce a stable oxide layer on the nanoparticles.
High-temperature annealing will improve structural stability relative to as-synthesized, unannealed nanoparticles.
High-temperature annealing will improve chemical stability relative to as-synthesized, unannealed nanoparticles.
High-temperature annealing will reduce oxidation rates relative to the unannealed baseline.
High-temperature annealing will reduce corrosion rates relative to the unannealed baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies within 773–1173 K, in inert gas or vacuum, for multi-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Impurities and defects may affect oxide-layer formation and stability.
An oxide-layer thickness below 1 nm is a criterion for failure to form the proposed stable barrier.
A corrosion rate above 10^-5 g/m^2/h is a criterion for falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies inert gas or vacuum but predicts formation of an oxide layer without specifying an oxygen source or controlled oxygen activity. This makes the proposed intervention-to-mediator link internally inconsistent or at least incomplete.
Reduced oxidation and corrosion rates are central predicted outcomes and falsification criteria, but the listed measurements are only XPS and TEM and do not directly measure either rate.
